1.meaning: An oath: 'By time!' Allah swears by al-ʿaṣr — sweeping, fleeting time itself: the ages of history, the passing era, the hours and seasons of a human life that drain away and never return (some early scholars, such as Zayd bin Aslam, read it more narrowly as the late-afternoon/evening hour, when daylight is visibly running out, though the broader sense of 'time' is the prevailing view). The opening wa- is the oath-particle (qasam) by which one solemnly swears, equivalent to 'By…!' — and an oath in the Qur'an signals that something weighty and urgent is about to be declared.
1.grammar: Here wa- is the particle of oath ('By…!'), not the ordinary 'and.' Grammatically it works as a governing particle (harf jarr) — the same class as prepositions — and any noun it governs is put in the genitive (majrūr) case. That is why this word ends in -i (the kasra): ʿaṣr-i, 'by THE time.' So 'swearing an oath' is the meaning wa- carries; assigning the genitive is what it does as a harf jarr. The final -i is therefore just the case forced by the particle, not a separate sense of 'of.' al- is the attached definite article 'the.'
1.root: ع-ص-ر (ʿ-ṣ-r) — to press/squeeze out (as juice is pressed); from it ʿaṣr, the portion of the day being 'pressed' to its end, hence the late afternoon and, more broadly, time and the passing age.

1.meaning: An emphatic opening particle. It carries no single English word; it injects certainty into the whole sentence, like saying 'It is an established truth that...' or 'Indeed, without doubt...'. It assures the listener that what follows is real and reliable.
1.grammar: A particle of emphasis and confirmation. Grammatically it governs the noun after it, forcing that noun ('the human being') into the accusative case — which is exactly why the next word ends in -a (al-insāna). It does not translate as a word so much as a tone of absolute certainty laid over the sentence.

2.meaning: The human being / humankind as a species. The 'al-' makes it generic, so it points not to one person but to humanity as a whole, every son and daughter of Adam.
2.grammar: Definite noun ('al-' = 'the'), here used to mean the whole human race. It is the topic the sentence makes a statement about (the ism of 'inna'). Normally such a subject would take the nominative, but the particle 'inna' before it overrides that and puts its noun into the accusative — which is why the word ends in -a (al-insāna) rather than the usual -u. So this is the logical subject, yet it is grammatically marked accusative because 'inna' demands it.
2.root: أ-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — to be sociable, familiar, human

3.meaning: A two-part phrase meaning 'is surely within / immersed in'. It combines an emphatic 'truly' with the preposition 'in', stressing that the human being is genuinely enclosed inside the state named next.
3.grammar: Two pieces joined together. The prefix 'la-' is the 'lām of emphasis' that pairs with 'inna' from word 1 to double down on the certainty ('inna... la...' = 'most surely'). 'fī' is the preposition 'in', and it puts the following noun into the genitive case, which is why 'loss' next ends in -in. There is no verb 'is' in the Arabic; it is understood.

4.meaning: Loss, ruin, deficit — the state of having squandered something precious and ending up worse off. Pictured like a failed business deal where one's capital (here, one's very life and time) drains away with nothing gained. The form here is indefinite, suggesting an awful, unspecified magnitude of loss.
4.grammar: Indefinite noun. The ending -in does two jobs at once: the -i part is the genitive case (required because the preposition 'fī' came before it, 'in [a state of] loss'), and the final -n sound (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite ('a loss', not 'the loss'). Leaving it indefinite hints at a loss so vast it is left undefined.
4.root: خ-س-ر (kh-s-r) — to lose, suffer loss, be ruined

1.meaning: A particle of exception meaning 'except' or 'save for.' It carves out a group from the sweeping statement just made (that all humanity is in loss), signalling that the people about to be described are the one exception to that universal ruin.
1.grammar: This is an indeclinable exception particle (it never changes its ending). It does not carry case itself; instead it introduces the excepted group that follows, telling you 'everyone is in loss — apart from these.'

2.meaning: 'Those who' — a masculine plural relative pronoun that points to a specific group of people and then attaches a description to them ('the ones who...'). It gathers up the believers who form the exception.

parts.en: the (relative marker; its lām is doubled)

2.grammar: A masculine plural relative pronoun, 'those who.' Its form is fixed (it does not change for case here); the -īna shape marks it as plural and masculine. The shadda over the lām in الَّذِيۡنَ means the lām is doubled, so the two parts reconstruct as al-l + dhīna = alladhīna. It sets up a relative clause: whatever verb comes next describes these people.

3.meaning: 'They believed / came to have faith' — they put their trust and conviction in Allah and accepted the truth in their hearts. The verb describes faith not as a passing thought but as a settled, embraced belief.
3.grammar: A past-tense (form IV) verb. Form IV (the lengthened a- at the start, originally 'a-) here carries the sense 'to come to believe, to have faith.' The -ū ending means the subject is 'they' (a group of males, or a mixed group). So: 'they believed.'

4.meaning: The connector 'and,' joining the next action (doing righteous deeds) to the one before it (believing). It links faith and action together as a paired description of the saved group.
4.grammar: A simple joining particle, 'and.' It has no case ending of its own; it merely couples what follows to what came before, here adding a second quality to the believers. (Note: in this source the transliteration 'waʿamilū' bundles this 'and' together with the following verb 'they did.')

5.meaning: 'They did / worked' — they performed and carried out actions. Paired with the following word, it means they put their faith into practice through deeds.
5.grammar: A past-tense (form I) verb, 'they did/worked.' The -ū ending marks the subject as 'they' (masc. plural). It governs the next word as its object: 'they did [the righteous deeds].'

6.meaning: 'The righteous deeds / good works' — actions that are sound, upright, and pleasing to Allah. The definite article ('the') points to the whole class of such good deeds.
6.grammar: A sound feminine plural noun/adjective, 'the righteous deeds,' acting as the object of 'they did.' Its ending is -āti (with kasra on the tā'). For sound feminine plurals this same -āti ending serves BOTH the accusative and the genitive — the ending alone does not distinguish the two cases. Here the word is accusative, but that is known from its syntactic role (object of ʿamilū, 'they did'), not from a distinct case marker. So: 'they did the good deeds.'
6.root: ص-ل-ح (ṣ-l-ḥ) — to be sound, upright, good

7.meaning: 'And they urged one another / counselled each other' — they mutually encouraged and advised one another. The form stresses that this is a two-way, reciprocal exchange, not one person lecturing another.
7.grammar: 'And' + a past-tense (form VI) verb. Form VI (the ta- prefix with the lengthened -ā-) signals a reciprocal action done back and forth between people: 'they advised one another.' The plural 'they' ending (here written -aw) marks the subject as a group. It is completed by the next word, which tells you what they urged each other toward.

8.meaning: 'To the truth / regarding the truth' — al-ḥaqq is what is real, right, and true: established truth and what is genuinely due. This is the first thing the believers urge upon one another.
8.grammar: The particle bi- ('with/to') joined to 'the truth.' Because bi- is a preposition, the noun after it takes the genitive case, shown by the final -i (ḥaqqi). It links back to the verb 'urged one another,' answering 'urged each other to/with what?' — namely, the truth.
8.root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q) — truth, right, what is real and due

9.meaning: 'And they urged one another to patience' — the believers also mutually counsel each other to ṣabr: steadfast endurance, perseverance through hardship, and self-restraint in holding firm to what is right. This repeats the reciprocal verb and names patience as its object.
9.grammar: 'And' + the same reciprocal form VI verb 'they urged one another' (ta- prefix, lengthened -ā-, plural 'they' ending), followed by bi- ('to/with') plus 'the patience.' After the preposition bi-, the noun takes the genitive case, marked by the final -i (ṣabri). The whole phrase parallels the previous one: 'and they urged one another to patience.'
9.root: ص-ب-ر (ṣ-b-r) — to be patient, endure, persevere
